text: NetFlow's record said 5.1 megabytes moved between two hosts over 41 seconds — the label on the envelope, not what's inside it. Deep packet inspection opens the envelope: it examines the actual payload content crossing a device, the same depth you read by hand in Wireshark's packet details and bytes panes, except done automatically, inline, at full network speed.

Where NetFlow can only say who talked to whom, how much, and for how long, DPI can say what the application actually did. The same traffic NetFlow logged as five megabytes over port 445 might turn out, under DPI, to be a routine file copy — or, in a more alarming case, traffic that looks like ordinary DNS but is actually carrying encoded data disguised inside it.

That thoroughness isn't free. Inspecting payload content means buffering packets, reassembling them into application-layer data, and examining the actual bytes — work far heavier than reading a header field in passing. Running full DPI on every link across a large network at full speed isn't realistic, which is why it typically lives at specific chokepoints like a perimeter firewall rather than everywhere a flow collector can sit cheaply.

In practice, a SOC doesn't pick one tool over the other. Flow data gives broad, always-on visibility across the whole network cheaply enough to watch continuously. The moment something in that flow data looks off — an unfamiliar destination, an unusual volume — that's the trigger to pull that one host's traffic under DPI for a detailed look at what's actually inside it.

Flow analysis tells you where to look. DPI tells you what's actually there once you're looking — together they cover both the breadth a whole network needs and the depth one suspicious host deserves. Next up: baselining normal traffic, so you know what 'unusual' even means before either tool can flag it.
